lines.text: Why doesn't an induction stove burn your hand?
Put your hand on an induction cooktop that's switched on. It's cold.
Put an iron pan in the same spot, and within seconds you can't touch it.
And under the glass, nothing is hot. Not before, not after.
Underneath is a copper coil.
Alternating current runs through it, flipping direction tens of thousands of times a second, faster than you can hear.
And with it, a magnetic field flips back and forth.
The glass top doesn't conduct and isn't magnetic. The field passes straight through it.
Above it sits the bottom of the pan. A changing field inside a metal pushes its electrons in circles. These are eddy currents.
And iron resists letting them flow. That resistance is heat.
The heat doesn't travel to the pan. The pan is the resistance.
That's why not every pot works. At that frequency, the current doesn't spread out. It crowds at the surface.
In iron, it's squeezed into a fraction of a millimeter, where it meets a lot of resistance.
In aluminum, the layer is several times thicker, and the metal conducts far better. The current barely meets resistance.
Hence the magnet test.
The coil below would suffer the same fate, so it isn't solid wire. It's hundreds of fine, insulated, twisted strands.
The effect that cooks on top is the enemy below.
Your hand was in that same field. But it isn't magnetic, and it conducts electricity more than ten million times worse than iron.
Induced heat depends on how well you conduct. With that number: zero.
And the cooktop won't even switch on unless it detects a pot.
The glass does end up hot, but later, and by contact. That's why it warns you about leftover heat.
And a knife left on top heats up too. The field doesn't tell objects apart. It tells materials apart.
The heat doesn't reach the pan. It's born inside it.
